# Axalta Coating Systems (AXTA) — Event Dossier
### Forensic interrogation of the catalyst, not the franchise
**Prepared 3 August 2026. All prices and filings verified on the open web as of that date.**

Axalta is in this file for one reason: it agreed on 18 November 2025 to merge with Akzo Nobel N.V., the Dutch coatings group, in an all-share deal. Our job is not to grade the paint business. It is to answer four questions: is the event real and binding, when does it actually pay, what is the price of the event today, and what backstops the shares if it fails.

The short answer is that the event is real and the price already reflects it. The opportunity our watch board recorded does not exist, and the reason is an arithmetic error we can name precisely.

---

## 1. THE EVENT — what is actually contracted

Each Axalta share converts into 0.6539 AkzoNobel ordinary shares. There is no cash element and no collar (a collar is a band that adjusts the exchange ratio if the acquirer's shares move; there is none here, so Axalta holders float with AkzoNobel's price). Axalta shareholders end up owning about 45% of the combined company; AkzoNobel holders about 55%. The combined group would have roughly $17 billion of revenue and an enterprise value near $25 billion.

The term that matters most, and the one our board omitted: **immediately before completion, AkzoNobel pays a special cash dividend of €2.5 billion to its own shareholders only** — reduced by whatever regular and interim dividends AkzoNobel has already paid in 2026. Axalta holders receive none of it. Economically, Axalta holders are buying into AkzoNobel *after* roughly a quarter of its market value has been paid out to the other side.

The companies net this out themselves. In the merger prospectus they state that, with AkzoNobel at €59.94 and the euro at $1.138 on 23 June 2026, the implied value of the consideration to an Axalta holder was **about $34.36 per share** — not the roughly $44.60 a naive multiplication of price times ratio would produce. The gap, about €13.77 per AkzoNobel share, is the pre-completion distribution. That single line is the whole story of this file.

**Milestones verified:**

| Date | Event | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 18 Nov 2025 | Definitive merger agreement signed | Done |
| 26 Jan 2026 | Pre-notification talks opened with the European Commission | Done |
| 20 Feb 2026 | US Federal Trade Commission issues a "second request" (a full antitrust investigation, not a formality) | Open |
| 23 Jun 2026 | US registration statement (Form F-4) declared effective by the SEC | Done |
| 16 Jul 2026 | Reported that the parties had still **not** formally notified the European Commission | Open |
| 23 Jul 2026 | Governance terms enhanced after shareholder dialogue; meetings unaffected | Done |
| 28 Jul 2026 | Axalta reports record second-quarter earnings | Done |
| **5 Aug 2026** | **Both shareholder votes — Axalta special meeting and AkzoNobel extraordinary meeting** | **Two days away** |
| Late 2026 – early 2027 | Company-guided completion window | Guidance, not a contract |
| **18 May 2027** | **Contractual outside date, extendable to 18 November 2027** | The only binding deadline |

Note what is *not* on that list: the 31 December 2026 hard date our board recorded. It appears in no merger document. The companies guide to "end of 2026 or beginning of 2027," and the enforceable deadline is more than nine months later than the board assumes — potentially fifteen months later if extended.

---

## 2. IS THE CATALYST BINDING? — the credibility test

**Strongly binding on the terms; weakly bound on the timing.** These are different things and the distinction is where the money is.

*What is genuinely locked:* a signed definitive agreement, a fixed exchange ratio, no financing condition whatsoever (the consideration is stock, so no lender can walk), an effective registration statement, unanimous board support on both sides, no competing offer on the table, and a governance package that has been amended once already to answer objecting holders. The chief financial officer succession is settled — Axalta's Carl Anderson takes the combined role — which is a meaningful tell that both sides expect this to happen.

*What is not locked:* when. Clearances are needed in roughly thirty jurisdictions. Three matter: the US Federal Trade Commission, the European Commission, and the UK Competition and Markets Authority. The FTC's second request has been outstanding since February. On the European side, the parties opened informal talks in January but had still not filed the formal notification as of mid-July — and a European Phase 1 review runs twenty-five working days *from formal notification*, with an in-depth Phase 2 adding roughly ninety more. Trade reporting has flagged powder coatings as the overlap most likely to force an in-depth probe and structural remedies, meaning divestitures. Vehicle refinish paint — the collision-repair market where both firms are leaders — is the obvious second pressure point.

Put plainly: on 3 August 2026, with the votes two days away, the European clock has probably not started. A completion "at the end of 2026" requires a clean, single-phase European review notified almost immediately. That is possible. It is not what the reporting suggests.

---

## 3. MANAGEMENT AND SPONSOR CREDIBILITY

Axalta's own execution is not the risk here, and the record is good. The second quarter reported on 28 July 2026 was the strongest in the company's history: net sales just under $1.35 billion, up about 3% from a year earlier; adjusted operating cash profit (adjusted EBITDA — earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation) of $305 million at a 22.7% margin, both records; adjusted earnings per share of $0.72, up 13% and ahead of the $0.65 the street expected; $107 million of free cash flow; $80 million of gross debt repaid; and net borrowings down to 2.2 times cash profit, the lowest in the company's life as a public company. Full-year guidance was held, not cut: low-single-digit sales growth, $1.14 to $1.17 billion of adjusted cash profit, $2.55 to $2.70 of adjusted earnings per share, and free cash flow above $500 million. Third-quarter guidance of $295 to $305 million of cash profit is consistent with it.

That is a management team delivering into a merger rather than coasting, and it earns credibility. It does not, however, speak to the question that decides this trade — which is whether antitrust regulators in Brussels and Washington move fast and clean, and neither management controls that.

AkzoNobel's own trading is softer: first-half revenue fell about 5%, with currency taking two points and the sale of its Indian liquid-coatings business three. Since Axalta holders are being paid in AkzoNobel stock, that softness is now our exposure, not somebody else's. The synergy claim — "north of $600 million" of annual cost savings, roughly 90% of it inside three years after closing — is credible in a business this overlapping, but it is a 2028 fact, not a 2026 one.

**Guidance reliability: High** on the operating business. **Medium** on the regulatory timetable, where the parties have consistently guided to a window they have not yet earned the right to promise.

---

## 4. THE DOWNSIDE FLOOR — what actually backstops the price

**Verified floor: about $28.18 per share.** Two independent checks agree, and one important caveat applies to both.

*The market's own undisturbed mark.* Axalta closed at **$28.18 on 17 November 2025**, the last session before the merger leaked into the tape (confirmed against the price history; the shares gapped to $28.00 on the 18th on six times normal volume). That is the price at which the market, with full knowledge of the business and none of the deal, valued the company. On this year's guided cash profit and roughly $2.44 billion of net borrowings across 214.0 million shares, $28.18 works out to about 7.3 times enterprise value to cash profit — a defensible level for a coatings business, not a distressed one.

*The parts, valued independently.* Performance Coatings — refinish paint sold to collision-repair body shops, plus industrial coatings — did $3.28 billion of 2025 revenue and carries the bulk of the profit, call it roughly $870 million of cash profit. Mobility Coatings — paint sold to vehicle manufacturers for new cars — did $1.84 billion at roughly $285 million. Refinish deserves a premium multiple because it is genuinely sticky: body shops are locked in by colour-matching systems, dispensing equipment and trained technicians. Mobility deserves a discount: it is cyclical, competitive and tied to build rates. At 9 times and 5 times respectively, enterprise value is about $9.3 billion; net of borrowings that is roughly **$31.90 per share**. Stretch Performance to 9.5 times and you reach about $34.60.

*The caveat that matters most:* **this is a valuation floor, not a contractual one.** The deal is all stock. Nobody pays Axalta shareholders anything if it breaks. There is no cash backstop, no termination payment flowing to holders, no reverse break fee protecting us. If the merger fails, the shares find their own level — and because the shareholder register has rotated heavily to merger-arbitrage funds who own the stock only for the spread, that unwinding would likely overshoot below $28 before recovering toward the low thirties. So the honest reading is: an initial air-pocket to roughly $28, a recovery value nearer $31 to $32, and no contract anywhere in the chain.

*What supports the floor:* a clean balance sheet with no going-concern question, no share-issuance programme, no covenant stress, no financing contingency, ample liquidity, record-low leverage and free cash flow guided above $500 million.

*What erodes it:* soft end-market demand keeping guidance at the low end, tariff and raw-material uncertainty flagged on the second-quarter call, and the slow structural drag of collision-avoidance technology on body-shop paint volumes. None of these is terminal. All of them argue against paying up.

---

## 5. THE PRICE OF THE EVENT TODAY — the board's arithmetic error

Our watch board recorded a live price of $32.34 against a target of $42.64, a spread of about 32% and a reward-to-risk of 2.48 to 1. **That target is wrong, and it is wrong in a way we can reconstruct exactly.** $42.64 divided by the 0.6539 ratio and the exchange rate implies AkzoNobel at roughly €56.6 — in other words, the target was the ratio multiplied by AkzoNobel's share price, with the €2.5 billion distribution left out entirely. Axalta last closed at **$35.81** (Friday 31 July; the shares have not yet traded since AkzoNobel's move today). So the terms are worth roughly $0.53 more than the last print — a gross spread of about **1.5%**, which will very likely be gone by this morning's open, since Axalta has yet to mark AkzoNobel's 2.1% rally. On Friday's own closing marks the spread was slightly *negative*: the stock traded a touch through the terms.

Against that: a fall to $28.18 is **−21.3%**. Roughly one and a half percent of upside against a fifth of capital. The board recorded 2.48 to 1 in our favour; the true figure is closer to **0.07 to 1 against**.

And the spread is not even ours to keep. Professional arbitrageurs capture a fixed-ratio stock spread by shorting the acquirer. This book cannot. Buying Axalta here is functionally an unhedged long position in a euro-denominated Dutch share, exposed to both AkzoNobel's price and the dollar-euro rate, for a spread of about one percent over a wait of five to sixteen months.

| Term | Detail |
|---|---|
| Consideration | 0.6539 AkzoNobel ordinary shares per Axalta share. No cash alternative, no collar (a collar is a band that adjusts the ratio if the buyer's stock moves). |

Back-solving the 23 June figure gives a distribution deduction of about €13.76 per AkzoNobel share — roughly 23% of AkzoNobel's market price. Applying the same method to today: AkzoNobel at €59.26 (27 July 2026), less €13.76, times 0.6539, times a euro/dollar rate of 1.1384, gives **$33.87 per Axalta share**.

Axalta last closed at **$32.76** on 24 July 2026, up 3.4% that session. So:

- Gross spread to the deal's own value: **+3.5%**
- Drop to the undisturbed pre-announcement price of $28.17 (17 November 2025): **−14.0%**
- Reward-to-risk: **about 0.25 to 1**
- Completion probability the market is implying: (32.76 − 28.18) ÷ (33.87 − 28.18) = **about 80%**

An 80% implied completion probability against a 3.5% spread over a five-to-sixteen-month wait is an ordinary, fully-functioning merger-arbitrage price. There is no mispricing here to harvest. The market has done this arithmetic; our board did not.

One further structural point that removes the "fixed payout" comfort entirely: because the consideration is shares with no collar and no cash, **there is no ceiling and no guaranteed number**. An Axalta holder is, in economic substance, long 0.6539 AkzoNobel shares with a 3.5% carry attached. If AkzoNobel falls 15%, so does the Axalta payoff. There is also unhedged currency risk, since the consideration is a euro-denominated security.

## 4. How credible are the sponsors on hitting the date?

High on intent and execution, moderate on timing.

**Green flags.** Both boards unanimously recommend the deal and have reaffirmed it repeatedly. There is no financing condition — this is stock, not a leveraged buyout, so no lender can walk. AkzoNobel has nonetheless pre-funded the special distribution with €600 million and €750 million of new senior notes plus a €1.5 billion revolving facility, which means the cash condition is already solved rather than aspirational. Cevian Capital, an activist holding roughly 5% of AkzoNobel, supports the combination. Competing suitors for AkzoNobel withdrew in June, removing the risk that AkzoNobel's board gets distracted or diverted. And the registration statement went effective on schedule, which is a genuine, checkable milestone rather than a promise.

**Red flags.**
- **The antitrust overlap is the real one.** AkzoNobel and Axalta are both top-tier players in vehicle refinish — the paint sold to collision-repair body shops. This is a concentrated global market, and it is precisely the kind of horizontal overlap that draws remedies. The US Federal Trade Commission's second request, issued 20 February 2026, confirms this is not a formality. Management's own language is telling: they concede "there are areas where at some point we may be discussing remedies," which "can be behavioural remedies… or selective divestments." Filings are pending in roughly 30 countries; any one of them can slow the clock.
- **Timing has already been quietly stretched.** A merger Q&A earlier in 2026 described a "mid-July 2026" shareholder vote and a "year-end 2026" close. The vote landed on 5 August, and the guided close is now "late 2026 to early 2027." That is a modest slip, not a collapse, but it points in the wrong direction.
- **Axalta shareholders are not being paid a premium, and some of them have noticed.** The consideration on the day before announcement was about $30.25 against an undisturbed price of $28.17 — roughly a 7% premium, which is negligible for a change of control. Artisan Partners Global Value (about 0.7% of Axalta) publicly urged holders to reject the deal. Shapiro Capital Management (about 1.1%, a top-25 holder) said it was "very disappointed" and would vote against unless terms improved or alternatives were explored. The 23 July governance amendment — annual director re-election after three years instead of five, and a two-thirds rather than three-quarters board threshold for senior appointments — is a concession, but it is governance, not price. No shareholder who objects to being paid nothing for control has been given anything for control.
- **The vote threshold has a trap door.** Axalta's approval requires a simple majority of votes cast *only if* an accompanying bye-law amendment passes. If that amendment fails, the merger needs a **three-quarters** majority. With two vocal opponents already on the record, that is a low-probability but genuinely fatal branch, and it resolves in nine days.

## 5. The verified downside floor — what actually backstops the price

There is no contractual floor. This is a stock-for-stock merger; there is no cash backstop, no minimum value, and no termination payment flowing to shareholders. The floor is a valuation floor, and it has to be built from the standalone business.

**Anchor one — the undisturbed price.** Axalta closed at **$28.17** on 17 November 2025, the last trading day before the deal was public. On this year's guidance that is about 7.4 times enterprise value to adjusted earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EV/EBITDA — the company's value including debt, divided by its cash operating profit). This is the number our board carries as the floor, and it is a defensible one.

**Anchor two — the standalone parts.** Axalta reports two segments. In 2025, Performance Coatings (refinish plus industrial) did $3.28 billion of revenue and Mobility Coatings (light-vehicle and commercial-vehicle original equipment) did $1.84 billion. I estimate segment cash operating profit of roughly $0.83 billion and $0.28 billion respectively, consistent with the $1.11 billion company total. Valuing Performance at 9 times and Mobility at 5 times gives an enterprise value of about $8.9 billion; less net debt of $2.54 billion at 31 March 2026, that is about **$29.60 per share** on 214.0 million shares. A mid-case at 9.5 and 5.5 times gives about $32.20; a generous case at 10.5 and 6 times gives about $36.70.

The two anchors agree: a break sends the stock to something in the **high-$20s**, call it $28. In practice it would likely trade slightly below that on the first day as merger-arbitrage funds unwind in a hurry, then recover toward standalone fair value. So the floor is real but soft — a valuation level that depends on the coatings cycle holding, not a contractual payment that arrives regardless.

**What supports it.** The underlying business is sound and cash-generative. Management guides 2026 to $1.14–1.17 billion of adjusted cash operating profit, adjusted earnings per share of $2.55–2.70, and free cash flow above $500 million. Liquidity at the end of the first quarter was $608 million of cash plus $770 million of undrawn revolver, and the company prepaid $50 million of term loans. Net debt of $2.54 billion is about 2.2 times cash operating profit — comfortable. There is no going-concern issue, no equity issuance programme, no covenant stress, and no financing contingency. On the standard forensic red-flag checklist for event names, Axalta is clean.

**What erodes it.** Guidance is drifting toward the low end on softer demand, and the refinish franchise has a slow structural headwind: collision-avoidance technology reduces accident frequency, which reduces the volume of paint body shops buy. That is a decade-long drag, not a cliff, and it is partly offset by a growing vehicle fleet and more expensive repairs per claim.

## 6. Governance and process integrity

Nothing here suggests a manipulated process, but the shape of the deal deserves naming plainly. A "merger of equals" with no premium, where the larger party pays itself €2.5 billion in cash on the way out and the smaller party receives shares only, is a structure that transfers value toward the acquirer's register. Axalta's holders end up owning 45% of the combined company and 45% of the $600 million of synergies — which, capitalised, is worth roughly $10 per Axalta share if delivered — but they surrendered control to get it, and control normally carries a price. The objecting shareholders are making a coherent argument, not a nuisance one. That said, at 1.8% of the register between them, they lack the votes to block on a simple-majority test.

## 7. What the market is not arguing about

There is no meaningful disagreement left to exploit. The deal has been public for eight months, the terms are fixed and published, the prospectus is effective, both meeting dates are set, the objectors have said their piece in public, and the price sits within a few percent of the terms. This is the opposite of a mispriced special situation: it is a crowded, well-understood arbitrage where the residual return is compensation for regulatory tail risk and for tying up capital, and where our book — which cannot short AkzoNobel to lock the ratio — would be taking the euro-equity risk without the hedge that makes the trade work for professional arbitrageurs.

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict

The event is credible and on track; the recorded opportunity is not. Everything that can be verified about the merger points to a well-run, well-supported, likely-to-complete transaction — and precisely because it is all of those things, the market has already paid for it. The board's 32% spread is an artifact of omitting the €2.5 billion pre-completion distribution from the target price. Corrected, the spread is 3.5% against a 14% drop to the undisturbed price, with the real deadline fifteen months away rather than five months, and with the payoff floating on a foreign share price we would not be hedging.

The one thing to weigh before sizing anything: **this is not a defined-risk special situation, it is an unhedged long position in AkzoNobel with a small carry.** If the investment case is "we want to own 45% of the world's number-two coatings company as it takes out $600 million of costs," that is a legitimate three-year proposition and should be argued on its merits, at a size and in a book appropriate to a cyclical industrial compounder. It should not be dressed as event arbitrage, because as event arbitrage the numbers do not work.

On the underlying franchise: refinish is a genuinely sticky business — body shops are locked in by colour-matching systems, equipment, and technician training, and they do not switch casually. That is a narrow but real competitive advantage, and it is stable rather than widening or collapsing. Mobility Coatings is far more commoditised and cyclical. The structural threat from safer vehicles is real but slow and manageable, not terminal. The cheapness on display, such as it is, is neither a fear-print nor a value trap — it is simply a fair price for a decent, cyclical, mid-quality industrial.
